questions.title: How an LLM actually generates a response
questions.prompt: Explain, in plain terms, what actually happens when an LLM generates a response to a prompt. What does 'autoregressive, next-token prediction' mean, and why does the model produce its answer one piece at a time instead of all at once?
questions.modelAnswer: An LLM generates text autoregressively: at each step, it takes everything generated so far (the prompt plus whatever tokens it has already produced) and computes a probability distribution over its entire vocabulary for what token should come next. It samples one token from that distribution, appends it to the sequence, and then repeats the exact same process -- recomputing a fresh distribution over the next token given the now-longer sequence -- until it produces a stop token or hits a length limit. There is no step where the model 'plans' the whole answer in advance; each token is chosen based only on the sequence that exists at that moment, which is why changing one early token (through sampling randomness) can send the rest of the response in a different direction.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd explain it to someone non-technical: the model isn't writing the whole answer and then showing it to you -- it's genuinely deciding one token at a time, where each decision is 'given everything written so far, what's the most likely next piece.' It picks a token, that token becomes part of the input for the next decision, and the cycle repeats. That's literally what 'autoregressive' means -- the model's own prior output feeds back in as input for the next step. The practical consequence I care about as an engineer is that this is also why streaming works the way it does -- you can show the user each token the moment it's produced, because the model really is finishing one piece before computing the next, not holding a complete answer back until the end.

Confusing next-token prediction with the model looking ahead or planning several tokens in advance

Treating 'token' and 'word' as interchangeable

questions.title: What a context window actually limits
questions.prompt: What is a context window, in concrete terms, and what actually happens when a conversation's total tokens exceed the model's context window limit?
questions.modelAnswer: A context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can take as input (and, depending on the provider, sometimes input plus output together) in a single request -- it includes the system prompt, every prior message in the conversation you send back, and the new user message, all counted as tokens, not characters or words. It is not memory in the sense of the model 'remembering' past turns on its own; every call is stateless, and the full conversation has to be resent each time. When the total tokens would exceed the window, the request either gets rejected with an error, or -- depending on how the calling application is built -- older messages get silently dropped or truncated to make room, which is why a long-running conversation can appear to 'forget' something that was said many turns earlier: it was never resent, not actually forgotten by the model.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe it as the model's working memory for a single request, not persistent memory across requests. Every single API call is stateless -- the model has no idea a previous call ever happened unless I resend the relevant history myself, and that entire history, plus the system prompt and the new message, all has to fit inside the context window's token budget. If I don't manage that budget, one of two things happens: the API just rejects the request outright because it's over the limit, or if my own application is responsible for trimming history before sending it, older turns get cut to make room. That second case is the one that actually confuses people in production -- the user experiences it as 'the assistant forgot what I said earlier,' but what really happened is my application dropped that message from the request before it ever reached the model.

Forgetting that the system prompt and all prior turns count against the same token budget as the new message

Confusing token count with word or character count when estimating what fits

questions.title: Why token count doesn't match word count
questions.prompt: What is a token in the context of an LLM, and why can't you reliably estimate token count by counting words? What problems does this cause if you get the estimate wrong?
questions.modelAnswer: A token is the unit a model's tokenizer actually breaks text into -- which is often a sub-word chunk, not a whole word: common words may be a single token, while longer, rarer, or non-English words can split into several tokens, and punctuation, whitespace, and even individual characters can each consume their own token depending on the tokenizer. Because the mapping between words and tokens varies by language, vocabulary, and the specific tokenizer a model family uses, a rough 'word count equals token count' assumption is only ever approximate, commonly cited as roughly four characters or three-quarters of a word per token in English -- and that ratio gets noticeably worse for code, non-English text, or text full of rare terms. Getting this wrong matters practically: underestimating tokens can cause a request to unexpectedly exceed the context window or a response to get cut off mid-generation, and it also throws off cost estimates, since API pricing is billed per token, not per word.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I think about it: a tokenizer doesn't split on spaces, it splits on whatever sub-word chunks it was trained to recognize, so 'token' and 'word' are just different units entirely. A common word might be one token, but something like a rare technical term or a word in a language the tokenizer wasn't tuned for can break into three or four tokens. In practice I use the rough rule of thumb -- around four characters per token in English -- as a sanity check, but if I actually need an accurate count before sending a request, I run the real tokenizer the provider ships rather than guessing, because being wrong about this isn't just a minor rounding error. If I underestimate and go over the context window, the call either fails outright or the response gets truncated mid-thought, and since billing is per token, a bad word-to-token assumption also means my cost estimates for a feature can be meaningfully off.

Not accounting for punctuation, whitespace, or code syntax also consuming tokens
Using a word-count estimate for a production system instead of running the actual tokenizer
Forgetting that token-based pricing means a bad estimate is also a cost-estimation error, not just a context-window risk

questions.title: Comparing model families at a glance
questions.prompt: An AI engineer needs to be able to orient quickly across the current model landscape. At a glance, what are the key dimensions you'd compare when looking at two different model families from two different providers, before writing a single line of integration code?
questions.modelAnswer: The dimensions that actually matter for an engineering decision, not just marketing claims, are: capability for the specific task (a family's flagship model and its smaller/cheaper variants can differ substantially on reasoning, coding, or instruction-following), context window size (which varies widely across families and directly constrains what you can send in one request), modality support (text-only versus vision or audio input), latency and throughput characteristics, pricing structure (input tokens and output tokens are typically billed at different rates, and that asymmetry matters for use cases with long inputs and short outputs or vice versa), and release/versioning cadence (how often the provider deprecates older model versions, since that affects long-term maintenance). A good comparison looks at the actual published documentation and benchmarks for the specific task at hand rather than a single generic leaderboard score, because a model that's strong on general knowledge isn't automatically the right choice for, say, structured data extraction or code generation.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I integrate anything, I pull up each provider's model documentation side by side and look at the same handful of things every time: what's the context window, because that alone can rule a model in or out for a document-heavy use case; what does it cost per million input tokens versus output tokens, since those are priced differently and my use case's input-to-output ratio changes which number actually matters more; does it support the modality I need, like images, since not every model in a family does; and how fast is it in practice, not just on paper, since a slower model can be a dealbreaker for a user-facing chat feature. I also always check the provider's own deprecation policy for that specific model version, because picking a model that's scheduled to be retired in three months creates work for me later that a newer model in the same family might avoid. I try not to lean on a single popular benchmark score, because the task I actually need to do rarely matches whatever that benchmark measured.

questions.title: Open-source vs. closed models, the real tradeoff
questions.prompt: What's the actual engineering tradeoff between using an open-source model you host yourself versus a closed model behind a provider's API? Don't just say 'control vs. convenience' -- be specific about what each side costs you.
questions.modelAnswer: A closed model behind a provider's API trades control for operational simplicity: you get a managed endpoint, automatic scaling, and the provider's own infrastructure and safety tuning, but you're dependent on their uptime, their pricing changes, their rate limits, and their deprecation schedule, and your data leaves your infrastructure for every request unless the provider offers a specific enterprise data-handling agreement. An open-source model you host yourself gives you data residency (nothing leaves your infrastructure), no per-token billing to a third party, and freedom to fine-tune or modify the model, but you now own the real cost of GPU infrastructure, the engineering effort to serve it reliably at the latency and throughput your product needs, and typically a capability gap versus the strongest closed frontier models for general-purpose reasoning tasks. The actual decision usually comes down to specific constraints: data sensitivity, predictable high-volume cost at scale favoring self-hosting, or needing the strongest possible general capability favoring a closed frontier model.
questions.professionalAnswer: I try to get past the generic 'control versus convenience' framing and ask what it actually costs in each direction. Going closed-API means I don't manage any GPU infrastructure, I get a model that's usually ahead on general capability, and scaling is someone else's problem -- but I'm now exposed to their rate limits, their pricing can change, and every request leaves my infrastructure, which can be a real blocker if I'm handling sensitive data without a specific data-processing agreement in place. Going open-source and self-hosted means I keep full control of data residency and I'm not paying per-token to anyone, but I've just taken on the job of actually running reliable inference infrastructure -- which is its own ongoing engineering cost, not a one-time setup -- and depending on the model I pick, I may be accepting a real capability gap versus the top closed models. In practice, I've seen the decision actually hinge on just one or two hard constraints -- like a client who can't let data leave their network, or a workload large enough that self-hosting is cheaper at scale -- rather than a philosophical preference either way.

questions.title: Why transformers replaced RNNs
questions.prompt: Conceptually, what was the real limitation of RNNs that made transformers such a major shift, rather than just an incremental improvement?
questions.modelAnswer: RNNs process a sequence step by step, carrying a hidden state forward from one token to the next, which creates two real problems: the processing is inherently sequential, so you can't parallelize it across a long sequence during training, and information from early in a long sequence has to survive being compressed and passed forward through every intermediate step, which in practice means it tends to fade -- the classic long-range dependency problem. Transformers replace that sequential hidden state with self-attention, which lets every token in the sequence directly attend to every other token in a single step, regardless of distance between them, and because that computation isn't inherently sequential, it can be parallelized across the whole sequence on modern hardware. That combination -- better handling of long-range dependencies and training that scales efficiently on GPUs -- is what actually let transformer-based models scale to the sizes and context lengths that produced today's LLMs, not just a modest accuracy bump over RNNs.
questions.professionalAnswer: The honest answer is it wasn't just 'better accuracy' -- it was a structural fix to two problems that were actually blocking progress. RNNs have to process a sequence one step at a time because each step depends on the previous hidden state, so you simply can't parallelize that across a long sequence during training, which makes training slow and limits how large a model you can practically train. Separately, information from early in a long sequence has to survive being squeezed through that same hidden state at every subsequent step, and in practice it degrades, so RNNs are genuinely bad at long-range dependencies. Self-attention in a transformer lets any token look directly at any other token in one step, so distance in the sequence stops being the problem it was for RNNs, and because that computation isn't sequential the way an RNN's is, it parallelizes well on GPUs. That's really the whole story of why transformers scaled into today's large models and RNNs didn't -- it's a training-efficiency and long-range-dependency fix, not just a tweak.

questions.title: Why accuracy alone can mislead
questions.prompt: Why can a model with 95% accuracy still be a bad, even useless, model? Walk through a concrete scenario where accuracy alone hides a real problem, and name a metric that would catch it.
questions.modelAnswer: Accuracy -- the percentage of predictions that were correct -- can be misleadingly high on imbalanced data: if a classification task has 95% of examples in one class and 5% in the other, a model that simply predicts the majority class every single time achieves 95% accuracy while having learned nothing useful about the minority class at all. For a task like fraud detection, where fraudulent transactions might be 1% of all transactions, a model that never flags fraud would be 99% accurate and completely useless. Precision and recall (and metrics built on them, like F1 score) catch this because they look specifically at how the model performs on the class that actually matters: recall asks what fraction of actual fraud cases were caught, and a 'predict majority class always' model would score zero on recall for the fraud class, immediately exposing the problem that overall accuracy hid.
questions.professionalAnswer: The example I always reach for is fraud or any rare-event detection, because it makes the problem obvious. If only 1% of transactions are actually fraud, a model that just predicts 'not fraud' for every single transaction is 99% accurate -- and completely worthless, because it catches zero fraud. That's the trap with accuracy on imbalanced data: it rewards the model for getting the majority class right, which is trivial, and says nothing about whether it's actually doing the hard, useful part of the job. What I'd look at instead is recall on the minority class specifically -- what fraction of the actual fraud did we catch -- and precision, to see how many of our fraud flags were real versus false alarms, and usually report F1 as the single number that balances both. Any time someone hands me a model's accuracy number without also showing me the class balance of the data, that's the first thing I ask about.

questions.title: Zero-shot vs. few-shot, and when to use each
questions.prompt: What's the difference between zero-shot and few-shot prompting, and what's the actual engineering tradeoff in choosing few-shot when zero-shot would also work?
questions.modelAnswer: Zero-shot prompting asks the model to perform a task with no worked examples in the prompt, relying entirely on the instruction and the model's pretrained knowledge; few-shot prompting includes a small number of example input/output pairs directly in the prompt before the real request, showing the model the exact pattern or format it should follow. Few-shot generally improves reliability and output-format consistency, especially for tasks with a specific structure (like a particular JSON shape or classification label set) that the model might guess differently each time under zero-shot. The tradeoff is real engineering cost, not just prompt length: every example consumes context-window tokens and therefore money on every single request, and if the examples are not representative of the actual input distribution, they can bias the model toward the examples' pattern in ways that hurt edge cases -- so the decision should be based on measured output quality and consistency, not a default assumption that more examples always helps.
questions.professionalAnswer: Zero-shot is just the instruction, no examples -- I'm trusting the model's training to already know the pattern I want. Few-shot means I'm showing it two or three concrete examples of input and expected output right in the prompt, which tends to lock in format and tone much more reliably, especially for anything with a specific output shape I need every time. The real tradeoff I weigh isn't really about prompting style -- it's cost and latency, because every example I add is tokens I'm paying for and sending on every single request forever, not just once. So my actual decision process is: start zero-shot, and only add few-shot examples if I measure that zero-shot's outputs are inconsistent enough to be a real problem. And when I do add examples, I pick ones that actually represent the range of inputs I expect in production, not just the easy cases, because a narrow set of examples can quietly bias the model toward a pattern that breaks on anything unusual.

questions.title: System prompt vs. user prompt, and why the split matters
questions.prompt: What's the actual difference between a system prompt and a user prompt in a chat completion API call, and why does putting an instruction in the wrong one cause real problems?
questions.modelAnswer: A chat completion request is built from messages with distinct roles: the system message sets persistent, standing instructions for how the assistant should behave across the whole conversation (its persona, constraints, output format rules), the user messages carry the actual request or turn-by-turn input, and the assistant messages carry the model's own prior replies, included when resending conversation history. Models are generally trained to weight system-level instructions more heavily and treat them as more durable than instructions embedded inside a user message, so putting a core behavioral rule (like 'always respond in valid JSON' or 'never reveal internal pricing') in the user message instead of the system message makes it more likely to drift or get overridden as the conversation continues, especially if a later user message contains conflicting instructions. The practical consequence of getting this wrong is inconsistent behavior across turns, not a hard failure, which makes it a subtle bug to track down.
questions.professionalAnswer: The system message is where I put anything that should hold true for the entire conversation -- the assistant's role, formatting rules, things it should never do -- and the user message is for the actual turn-by-turn ask. The reason I'm careful about this split isn't stylistic: models are generally trained to treat system-level instructions as more authoritative and durable, so a rule I actually need to hold for the whole session is safer there than buried in a user message, where it can get diluted or contradicted later if a user's own message happens to say something that conflicts with it. I've seen this go wrong in a subtle way -- a 'always output JSON' instruction stuffed into the first user turn instead of the system prompt works fine for a message or two, then quietly stops holding a few turns later once the conversation drifts, and it's a genuinely annoying bug to track down because it's not a hard failure, it's inconsistent behavior that only shows up intermittently.

questions.title: What actually makes an API RESTful
questions.prompt: What makes an API 'RESTful,' specifically? Name the actual constraints, not just 'it uses HTTP and returns JSON.'
questions.modelAnswer: REST is a set of architectural constraints, and the ones that matter day to day are: statelessness, meaning each request must contain all the information needed to process it, with no reliance on server-side session state between requests; a resource-based model, where URLs identify nouns (resources) like /users/123, and the HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) expresses the action on that resource rather than the URL encoding a verb; a uniform interface, where the same HTTP methods and status codes mean the same thing across every resource in the API; and representations, meaning the client interacts with a representation of a resource's state (commonly JSON) rather than the resource itself. Using HTTP and returning JSON is necessary but not sufficient -- an API that uses POST for everything regardless of the actual action, or that requires the server to remember a client's prior request to interpret the current one, is using HTTP without actually being RESTful.
questions.professionalAnswer: I push back a little when someone defines REST as just 'HTTP plus JSON,' because that's necessary but it's not what actually makes something RESTful. The constraints I actually check for are statelessness -- every request stands on its own, the server isn't tracking session state to interpret it -- and a resource-oriented URL structure, where the URL names a thing (a resource) and the HTTP verb says what I'm doing to it, so GET /orders/42 and DELETE /orders/42 point at the same resource but mean different actions. I also look for a uniform, predictable interface -- status codes and methods meaning the same thing everywhere in the API, not one endpoint returning 200 for an error and another returning 400 for the same kind of problem. An API that's technically HTTP but uses POST for every single operation, or that silently depends on server-side session state between calls, is using the transport without actually following the architecture, and that distinction matters because violating it is exactly what makes an API hard to reason about and cache correctly.

questions.title: Reading HTTP status codes from an AI API correctly
questions.prompt: When calling an AI provider's API, what's the practical difference in how your code should respond to a 429, a 500, and a 400 status code? Treating them all the same way is a common bug -- why?
questions.modelAnswer: These three status codes represent fundamentally different failure categories that call for different handling. A 429 (Too Many Requests) means the rate limit was exceeded, and the correct response is to retry after a delay -- typically honoring a Retry-After header if the API provides one, with exponential backoff if not -- because the request itself was valid and will likely succeed later. A 500-range error indicates a server-side failure on the provider's end, unrelated to anything wrong in your request, which also usually warrants a retry with backoff since it may be transient, but repeated 500s suggest escalating or falling back rather than retrying indefinitely. A 400 (Bad Request) means the request itself was malformed or invalid in some way your code controls -- a missing required field, an invalid parameter value -- and retrying the exact same request will simply produce the exact same 400 again; the correct response is to fix the request, not retry it. Treating all three the same (either always retrying or never retrying) either wastes time retrying a request that can never succeed, or gives up on transient failures that would have succeeded on retry.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat these as three different categories of problem, because conflating them is exactly the kind of bug that looks fine in testing and then causes real trouble in production. A 429 means I've been rate-limited -- the request was fine, I just need to back off and retry, ideally respecting a Retry-After header if the API sends one. A 500 means something broke on their end, not mine, and it's also usually worth a retry with backoff since it's often transient -- but if I keep getting 500s on the same call, blindly retrying forever isn't the right answer either, and I'd fall back or surface the failure instead. A 400 is different in kind, not just severity -- it means my request itself was invalid, so retrying the identical request will just get me the identical 400 again; what I actually need to do is fix the request. The bug I've seen bite people is writing one generic retry-with-backoff wrapper around every non-200 response, which means a malformed request burns through several retries doing nothing useful before finally giving up, instead of failing fast and loud the first time.

questions.title: Why bother with classes for an AI SDK wrapper
questions.prompt: A junior engineer asks why they should bother writing a class for their AI API wrapper instead of just writing a few standalone functions that call the API. What's your actual answer?
questions.modelAnswer: Standalone functions work fine for a one-off script, but once an AI integration needs to hold state across calls -- an API key, a configured base URL, a retry policy, a reusable HTTP session, accumulated usage/cost tracking -- that state has to live somewhere, and passing it as arguments to every single function call gets unwieldy and error-prone fast. A class lets you initialize that shared state once in __init__ and have every method access it through self, which keeps the calling code simple (client.chat(...) instead of chat(api_key, base_url, session, retry_policy, ...)) and keeps the configuration in one place instead of scattered across function signatures. It also gives you a natural place to add behavior later -- swapping in a mock client for tests, subclassing to support a second provider with a shared interface -- without changing every call site, which a pile of standalone functions sharing global state would make much harder to do safely.
questions.professionalAnswer: My honest answer is: for a genuinely one-off script, you probably don't need the class, and I wouldn't force it. But the moment this wrapper needs to hold onto anything across multiple calls -- the API key, a session object you don't want to recreate every time, retry settings, maybe a running token-usage counter -- a class gives that state one obvious home instead of forcing you to pass five arguments into every function or reach for global variables, which gets messy and bug-prone surprisingly fast. The other real win is swappability: if I wrap this in a class with a clean interface, I can hand my code a mock version of that client in tests without touching a real API, or later write a second class for a different provider that exposes the same methods, and nothing that calls client.chat(...) has to change. Standalone functions sharing implicit global state can technically do all of this too, but it gets fragile in a way a class with explicit instance state just doesn't.

Not mentioning that passing lots of shared config into every function call becomes unwieldy
Missing the testability benefit of being able to swap in a mock client
Overstating the case by claiming standalone functions can never work for this
keyPoints: A class gives shared state (API key, session, retry policy) one home instead of scattering it across function args
Calling code stays simple once configuration is set once in __init__
A class-based interface makes mocking for tests and supporting multiple providers much easier
The answer should be practical, not dogmatic -- a simple script may not need this

questions.title: Merge vs. rebase, conceptually
questions.prompt: What's the actual difference between git merge and git rebase when bringing a feature branch up to date with main, and what's the real tradeoff between them?
questions.modelAnswer: git merge takes the two branches' histories and creates a new merge commit that ties them together, preserving the exact history of both branches as they actually happened, including a visible merge point. git rebase instead takes your branch's commits and replays them one by one on top of the current tip of main, producing a linear history that looks as if you had branched off the latest main all along -- but it rewrites commit hashes in the process, which is the real tradeoff: rebase gives a cleaner, linear history that's easier to read later, but rewriting history on a branch that others have already pulled and based work on causes real problems for them, since their local history no longer matches. The practical rule is rebase is safe on a local or not-yet-shared branch to clean up history before opening a pull request, and merge (or at minimum, extreme caution) is the right call once a branch is shared with others.
questions.professionalAnswer: Merge preserves exactly what happened -- both branches' real commit history, tied together with a merge commit -- so you can always see that a merge happened and when. Rebase rewrites your branch's commits so they look like they were made on top of main's current tip, which gives you a clean, linear history, but it does that by actually creating new commits with new hashes, discarding the old ones. That's the real tradeoff: rebase's history is nicer to read, but rewriting history is dangerous the moment someone else has already pulled your branch and built on top of the old commits, because now their history and yours have diverged in a confusing way. My rule of thumb is simple -- rebase freely on my own branch before I've shared it with anyone, to clean things up before opening a PR, but once it's pushed and someone else might be working off it, I switch to merge, or I at least ask before rebasing something shared.
commonMistakes: Describing rebase as simply 'the same as merge but cleaner' without mentioning history rewriting
Not mentioning the real danger of rebasing a branch others have already based work on
Treating merge and rebase as interchangeable regardless of whether the branch is shared
Failing to describe what a merge commit actually preserves versus what rebase replays
keyPoints: Merge creates a merge commit preserving both branches' actual history
Rebase replays commits on top of main's tip, producing linear history but rewriting commit hashes
Rewriting shared history with rebase causes real problems for collaborators who already pulled it
Safe rule: rebase on unshared/local branches, merge (or caution) once a branch is shared

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what git merge does and preserves
Correctly explains what git rebase does, including history rewriting
Correctly identifies the danger of rebasing shared history

questions.title: Writing code to consume a streaming API response
questions.prompt: Write Python code that calls an LLM API with streaming enabled and prints each chunk of the response as it arrives, instead of waiting for the full response.
questions.modelAnswer: Streaming works by setting stream=True on the request and then iterating over the response as an iterable of chunks (the exact object shape depends on the SDK, but the pattern is consistent): each chunk typically contains a small delta of new content, which you extract and print or otherwise handle immediately, flushing output so it appears incrementally rather than all at once. The code must handle the case where a chunk doesn't contain new text (e.g. metadata-only chunks) by checking before accessing the content, and should accumulate the full text if the complete response is needed afterward for logging or further processing.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core pattern I always write is: enable streaming on the request, then loop over the response object chunk by chunk, pull out just the new text delta from each chunk, and print it immediately with flush so it actually shows up incrementally in the terminal instead of buffering. I also accumulate each delta into a full_response string as I go, because even though I'm streaming to the user, I usually still want the complete text afterward for logging or for passing into the next step of my pipeline.
questions.example:
full_response = ""

stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain backoff in one sentence."}],
    stream=True,
)

for chunk in stream:
    delta = chunk.choices[0].delta.content
    if delta:
        print(delta, end="", flush=True)
        full_response += delta

print()  # newline after streaming finishes
# full_response now holds the complete text for logging or further use
commonMistakes: Not checking whether a chunk actually contains new text before trying to use it, causing a crash on metadata-only chunks
Forgetting to flush output, so streamed text appears to arrive all at once anyway
Not accumulating the full response when it's needed afterward for logging or the next pipeline step
Setting stream=True but then calling a method that still waits for the entire response before returning
keyPoints: stream=True changes the response into an iterable of incremental chunks
Each chunk must be checked for actual content before being used
Printing with flush is required for the output to actually appear incrementally
Accumulating the full text alongside streaming is a common and useful pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly enables streaming on the request
Correctly iterates over chunks and extracts content safely
Handles flushing so output appears incrementally
Accumulates the full response for later use

questions.title: Writing a function/tool calling schema
questions.prompt: Write a valid tool/function-calling schema (the JSON structure you'd pass to an LLM API) for a tool called get_weather that takes a required city string and an optional unit parameter restricted to 'celsius' or 'fahrenheit'.
questions.modelAnswer: A function/tool calling schema needs a name, a clear natural-language description (which the model uses to decide whether and how to call the tool, so it matters more than it looks), and a parameters object following JSON Schema conventions: a type of 'object', a properties map defining each parameter's type and description, an enum constraining 'unit' to exactly the two allowed values, and a required array listing which parameters are mandatory -- here, just city, since unit is optional.
questions.professionalAnswer: The part people underestimate here is the description field -- it's not documentation for a human, it's the main signal the model uses to decide when to call this tool at all and how to fill in its arguments, so I write it like I'm explaining the tool to someone who can only read that one sentence. Structurally, parameters is just JSON Schema: type object, a properties map where each parameter gets its own type and description, an enum on unit so the model can't invent a third unit, and a required array that only lists city, since unit should be allowed to be omitted and defaulted by my own code.
commonMistakes: Writing a vague or missing description, which makes the model unreliable about when to call the tool
Marking unit as required even though the question specifies it's optional
Forgetting the enum constraint, letting the model pass an invalid unit value
Getting the overall schema shape wrong for the specific provider's expected format
keyPoints: The description field drives the model's decision to call the tool, not just human documentation
parameters follows JSON Schema conventions: type, properties, required
enum correctly restricts unit to only the two valid values
required correctly lists only the mandatory parameter (city)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Produces valid JSON matching a real tool-calling schema shape
Writes a clear, specific tool description
Correctly defines city as required and unit as optional
Correctly constrains unit with an enum

questions.title: Robustly parsing structured JSON output from an LLM
questions.prompt: Write Python code that requests structured JSON output from an LLM API and safely parses it, handling the case where the model returns text that isn't valid JSON.
questions.modelAnswer: Even with a provider's JSON mode or structured-output feature enabled, production code should not assume the returned text is always valid JSON -- it should wrap the parse in a try/except around json.loads, and on failure, log the raw text for debugging and either retry the request (optionally with a stricter instruction) or raise a clear, specific error rather than letting a JSONDecodeError propagate unhandled. When possible, validating the parsed object's actual shape (expected keys and types present) after parsing, not just that it parsed at all, catches the case where the model returns syntactically valid JSON that's still the wrong structure.
questions.professionalAnswer: Even when I turn on a provider's JSON mode, I still don't trust the output blindly -- I wrap the parse in a try/except around json.loads specifically, because a JSONDecodeError here is a real failure mode I've actually hit, not a theoretical one. If it fails, I log the raw text so I can see what the model actually returned, and then I either retry once with a more explicit instruction or raise a clear error that tells the caller exactly what happened, instead of letting a raw JSONDecodeError bubble up from somewhere deep in my code. And parsing successfully isn't the end of validation for me -- I also check that the parsed dict actually has the keys and types I expect, because the model can return syntactically valid JSON that's still missing a field my downstream code needs.
commonMistakes: Assuming JSON mode guarantees valid, well-formed JSON every time
Letting a JSONDecodeError propagate unhandled instead of catching and handling it explicitly
Parsing successfully but never validating that the expected keys/structure are actually present
Not logging the raw text on failure, making the error impossible to debug later
keyPoints: Structured output modes reduce but don't eliminate the chance of malformed JSON
json.loads should be wrapped in a try/except with a clear, specific failure path
Logging the raw text on failure is essential for debugging
Validating the parsed object's shape (keys/types) is a separate step from parsing successfully

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly requests structured/JSON output from the API
Wraps parsing in proper error handling
Validates the parsed structure's expected shape
Handles the failure case usefully (logging, clear error, or retry)

questions.title: Designing a minimal class-based AI API client wrapper
questions.prompt: Write a minimal Python class that wraps an AI provider's API client: it should store configuration in __init__ and expose a single ask(prompt) method that returns the model's text response.
questions.modelAnswer: The class should take configuration (API key, model name, and optionally base settings like temperature) in __init__ and store it as instance attributes, then initialize the underlying provider SDK client once, rather than recreating it on every call. The ask method should take the prompt text, build the actual API request using the stored configuration, extract just the text content from the response object (not the whole raw response), and return that clean string so calling code doesn't need to know the response's internal shape.
questions.professionalAnswer: I keep this intentionally minimal to start: __init__ takes whatever configuration this client needs -- API key, default model -- stores it on self, and creates the underlying SDK client once so I'm not paying setup cost on every call. Then ask(prompt) is the one public method callers actually use; internally it builds the request from self's stored config plus the new prompt, and importantly it returns just the clean text string, not the raw response object, because I don't want every call site in my codebase to need to know the exact shape of the provider's response.

Not storing the API key/config as instance state, requiring it to be passed into every method call

questions.title: Converting a plain class into a dataclass
questions.modelAnswer: A dataclass replaces the manual __init__ boilerplate with field declarations using type annotations, and the @dataclass decorator auto-generates __init__, a readable __repr__, and __eq__ for you. Regular methods like total_tokens stay exactly as they were, defined normally inside the class body -- the decorator only changes how the basic data-holding plumbing is generated, not how you write ordinary methods.
questions.professionalAnswer: The __init__ here was pure boilerplate -- assign four parameters to four attributes -- which is exactly what @dataclass exists to eliminate. I just declare each field with its type annotation at the class level instead of writing the constructor by hand, and I get __init__, a useful __repr__ for debugging, and __eq__ for free. The total_tokens method doesn't change at all -- it's a normal method and dataclasses don't touch anything except the data-holding parts of the class.
commonMistakes: Forgetting type annotations on the fields, which dataclasses requires
Still writing a manual __init__ alongside the @dataclass decorator, which is redundant
Not realizing regular methods like total_tokens require no change at all
Forgetting to import dataclass from the dataclasses module
keyPoints: @dataclass auto-generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ from annotated fields
Fields are declared with type annotations at the class level, not in a manual __init__
Ordinary methods are unaffected and written exactly as before
The result is less boilerplate with identical behavior

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly applies @dataclass with properly typed fields
Removes the manual __init__ entirely
Keeps total_tokens as a normal method, unchanged in behavior

questions.title: Making an authenticated POST request with requests
questions.prompt: Write Python code using the requests library that makes a POST request to an AI API endpoint, including a Bearer token in the Authorization header, a JSON body, and basic error handling for a non-200 response.
questions.modelAnswer: The requests.post call should pass the JSON body via the json= parameter (which serializes it and sets the Content-Type header automatically) and the API key via the headers dict as an 'Authorization': 'Bearer <key>' entry, never in the URL or body. After the call, check response.status_code (or call response.raise_for_status()) before trusting response.json(), since a non-200 response's body often isn't the expected success shape and calling .json() on it blindly, or trusting its fields, can produce a confusing downstream error instead of a clear one.
questions.professionalAnswer: A few things I always do here out of habit, because I've been burned by skipping them: I pass the body through json=, not data=, so requests handles serialization and sets the Content-Type header correctly for me, and the API key goes in the Authorization header as a Bearer token, never appended to the URL as a query parameter where it could end up in logs. After the call, I don't immediately call response.json() -- I check the status code first, because a non-200 response often has a completely different body shape (an error object, maybe not even JSON), and parsing it as if it were a success response gives me a confusing error far from the actual problem instead of a clear one right at the call site.
commonMistakes: Putting the API key in the URL as a query parameter instead of the Authorization header
Calling response.json() before checking whether the status code indicates success
Using data= instead of json=, requiring manual serialization and header management
Omitting a timeout, risking the request hanging indefinitely
keyPoints: The API key belongs in the Authorization header as a Bearer token, never in the URL
json= handles serialization and the Content-Type header automatically
Status code should be checked before trusting or parsing the response body
A timeout should be set to avoid an indefinitely hanging request

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly sets the Authorization Bearer header
Correctly sends the JSON body via json=
Correctly checks status code before trusting the response
Includes a timeout and raises a clear error on failure

questions.title: Calling multiple AI APIs concurrently with asyncio
questions.prompt: Write Python code using asyncio that calls an async AI API client for three different prompts concurrently and collects all three results, rather than calling them one after another.
questions.modelAnswer: Each individual call should be an async function awaiting the API client's async method, and the three calls should be wrapped as coroutines and passed to asyncio.gather, which runs them concurrently and returns their results in the same order they were passed in once all have completed. This is meaningfully different from calling await three times in sequence, which would wait for each call to fully finish before starting the next, turning three independent network calls into a strictly serial, slower operation.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mistake I watch for here is writing three separate await calls back to back, which looks like async code but actually runs completely sequentially -- each await blocks until that call finishes before the next one even starts, so you get zero concurrency benefit despite using asyncio. What actually gets concurrency is creating the three coroutines and handing them to asyncio.gather together, which kicks off all three network calls essentially at once and waits for all of them to finish, returning results in the original order. For something like three independent LLM calls that don't depend on each other, this is the difference between roughly the sum of all three latencies and roughly the slowest single one.
questions.example:
import asyncio

async def ask(client, prompt: str) -> str:
    response = await client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-mini",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

async def main(client):
    prompts = ["Summarize X", "Summarize Y", "Summarize Z"]
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(ask(client, p) for p in prompts))
    return results

# asyncio.run(main(client))
commonMistakes: Writing three sequential await calls, which runs them one after another instead of concurrently
Forgetting to use an async-capable client/method, mixing sync and async incorrectly
Not using asyncio.gather (or similar) to actually run the coroutines concurrently
Assuming results from gather come back in a different order than the inputs were passed
keyPoints: Sequential awaits do not provide concurrency, even though the code is technically async
asyncio.gather actually runs multiple coroutines concurrently
Results from gather preserve the original input order
This pattern meaningfully reduces total latency for independent API calls

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines an async function that awaits the API call
Correctly uses asyncio.gather for concurrent execution
Avoids the sequential-await anti-pattern
Code is valid and runnable

questions.title: Loading and running a pretrained Hugging Face pipeline
questions.prompt: Write Python code using the Hugging Face transformers library to load a pretrained sentiment-analysis pipeline and run it on a sample sentence.
questions.modelAnswer: The transformers library's pipeline() helper is the fastest way to use a pretrained model for a standard task: passing the task name ('sentiment-analysis') downloads a sensible default pretrained model and its matching tokenizer, wraps pre-processing, inference, and post-processing into one callable, and returns a simple list of results with a label and confidence score. Calling the resulting pipeline object directly with the input text is all that's needed to run inference -- no manual tokenization or model-loading code is required for this level of use.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is deliberately the easy path -- pipeline() is there specifically so I don't have to manually load a tokenizer and a model and wire them together myself for a standard task. I just call pipeline('sentiment-analysis'), which pulls a sensible default pretrained model for that task, and then I call the returned object directly on my text. It hands back a label and a confidence score, which is enough for a quick prototype or a straightforward classification need without writing any of the lower-level model-loading code myself.

from transformers import pipeline

classifier = pipeline("sentiment-analysis")
result = classifier("This new AI course is genuinely well put together.")

# [{'label': 'POSITIVE', 'score': 0.9987}]

questions.title: Writing a reusable few-shot prompt template
questions.prompt: Write a reusable few-shot prompt template (as a Python string template, not a one-off prompt) for classifying a piece of customer feedback as 'bug', 'feature-request', or 'praise'. Include at least two worked examples in the template.
questions.modelAnswer: A reusable template separates the fixed scaffolding (instructions, worked examples, output format) from the one variable part that changes per call (the new feedback text to classify), typically using a placeholder that gets filled in with .format() or an f-string at call time. The worked examples should cover at least one example per label where practical, be genuinely representative of real feedback rather than trivially easy cases, and the instructions should explicitly state the exact allowed output values so the model isn't guessing at the label vocabulary.
questions.professionalAnswer: I build this as a template string with one placeholder for the new input, so every call reuses identical instructions and examples and only the feedback text itself changes -- that consistency is the whole point of templating instead of writing a fresh prompt each time. I make sure the examples are varied enough to actually teach the distinction (a bug report, a feature ask, and ideally a thank-you/praise message), not three nearly-identical easy cases, and I explicitly spell out the three allowed labels in the instructions so the model has a fixed vocabulary to choose from instead of inventing its own phrasing.
questions.example:
FEEDBACK_CLASSIFIER_TEMPLATE = """Classify the following customer feedback as exactly one of: bug, feature-request, praise.

Example 1:
Feedback: \"The export button crashes the app every time I click it.\"
Label: bug

Example 2:
Feedback: \"It would be great if I could schedule reports to run automatically.\"
Label: feature-request

Example 3:
Feedback: \"Your support team fixed my issue in five minutes, amazing service.\"
Label: praise

Now classify this feedback:
Feedback: \"{feedback_text}\"
Label:"""

prompt = FEEDBACK_CLASSIFIER_TEMPLATE.format(feedback_text="The app is so slow after the last update.")

Including examples that are too similar to each other to actually teach the distinction between labels
Not explicitly stating the exact allowed output values, leaving label vocabulary ambiguous
Forgetting to cover most or all of the target labels with at least one example

Examples should be varied and representative, not trivially similar
The allowed output labels should be stated explicitly to constrain the model's vocabulary
Reusability is the actual goal, not a single well-crafted one-time prompt

questions.title: Resolving a merge conflict from the command line
questions.prompt: You run git merge and get a conflict in src/client.py. Walk through the actual git commands and steps you'd use to resolve it and complete the merge.
questions.modelAnswer: After the conflict is reported, open the conflicted file and look for git's conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>), which bracket the competing versions from each branch; edit the file by hand to keep the correct combined content and remove all three marker lines completely -- leaving a marker in place is a common mistake that breaks the file. Then stage the resolved file with git add, confirm there are no remaining conflicts with git status, and complete the merge with git commit (git merge typically pre-fills a merge commit message, which can be kept or edited). If the merge turns out to be a mistake partway through, git merge --abort cleanly backs out before committing.
questions.professionalAnswer: First I open the file and look for the three conflict markers -- <<<<<<< HEAD marks the start of my current branch's version, ======= separates it from the incoming branch's version, and >>>>>>> marks the end of theirs. I read both sides, decide what the correct final content actually is (which might be one side, the other, or a combination), and edit the file directly to that final state, making sure I delete all three marker lines -- leaving one in is a mistake I've made before and it's an easy one to miss since the file still looks mostly fine. Once it looks right, git add the file to mark it resolved, run git status to confirm nothing else is still conflicted, and git commit to finish the merge. If partway through I realize this merge is more complicated than I want to untangle right now, git merge --abort gets me back to a clean state before I've committed anything.
questions.example:
# After git merge reports a conflict in src/client.py:
# 1. Open src/client.py, resolve the <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>> sections by hand
# 2. Stage the resolved file
git add src/client.py

# 3. Confirm nothing else is still conflicted
git status

# 4. Complete the merge
git commit

# If you need to back out entirely before committing:
# git merge --abort

Forgetting to git add the resolved file before committing

Not knowing git merge --abort exists as a clean way to back out mid-conflict

git merge --abort cleanly backs out of an in-progress merge

questions.title: Writing a basic GitHub Actions workflow to run tests
questions.prompt: Write a basic GitHub Actions YAML workflow that runs a Python project's test suite automatically on every push.
questions.modelAnswer: A minimal CI workflow lives in .github/workflows/ as a YAML file, declaring a name, the on trigger (push, and typically pull_request too), and a jobs section with at least one job that runs on a specified runner image, checks out the repository code (actions/checkout), sets up the correct language runtime (actions/setup-python with a specified version), installs dependencies (commonly from requirements.txt), and finally runs the test command (e.g. pytest). Each of these is a separate step, run in order, and if any step fails the workflow run is marked failed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The skeleton I reach for every time has the same shape: trigger on push (and I'd normally add pull_request too, though the question only asked for push), one job targeting ubuntu-latest, and then steps in order -- checkout the repo with actions/checkout, set up the right Python version with actions/setup-python, install dependencies from requirements.txt, and finally run pytest. The thing that trips people up on a first attempt is forgetting the checkout step entirely, since without it the runner has no code to actually test.
questions.example:
name: Run Tests

on: [push]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install -r requirements.txt

      - name: Run tests
        run: pytest

Placing the workflow file outside the required .github/workflows/ directory

questions.title: Defensively parsing and validating a JSON API response
questions.prompt: Write Python code that takes a raw JSON string from an API response and safely extracts a nested field (data.user.email), handling the cases where the JSON is malformed or the expected keys are missing.
questions.modelAnswer: Safe extraction requires two separate layers of defense: first, parsing the raw string with json.loads inside a try/except for json.JSONDecodeError, since the string might not be valid JSON at all; second, after parsing succeeds, safely navigating the nested structure using .get() at each level (rather than direct key indexing with []), since any intermediate key might be missing, and .get() returns None instead of raising a KeyError, letting the code check for a missing value cleanly at the end rather than crashing partway through the chain.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat this as two separate failure modes, because conflating them produces confusing error messages. First, is the string even valid JSON -- that's a try/except around json.loads catching JSONDecodeError specifically. Second, assuming it parsed fine, does the nested path I need actually exist -- for that I chain .get() calls instead of direct bracket indexing, because .get() on a missing key returns None instead of blowing up with a KeyError, which lets me walk all the way down the chain safely and just check at the very end whether I actually got a value back, rather than wrapping every single level in its own try/except.
commonMistakes: Using direct key indexing (data['data']['user']['email']) instead of .get(), causing a KeyError on any missing level
Not catching JSONDecodeError, assuming the input string is always valid JSON
Wrapping every level of nested access in its own separate try/except instead of chaining .get()
Returning an unhelpful generic exception instead of a clean None or specific error for the missing-field case
keyPoints: Parsing failure (invalid JSON) and missing-key failure are two distinct cases to handle
json.JSONDecodeError should be caught explicitly around json.loads
Chaining .get() with default values safely navigates nested structures without raising KeyError
The function should return a clear, predictable result (e.g. None) rather than crashing on missing data

questions.title: Your app keeps getting rate-limited in production
questions.prompt: Your AI application starts throwing 429 errors in production under moderate load, even though it worked fine in testing. Walk through how you'd diagnose and fix this.
questions.modelAnswer: First confirm the actual rate limit tier and type you're hitting -- requests per minute, tokens per minute, or concurrent requests -- since providers often enforce several limits simultaneously and the fix differs depending on which one is being exceeded; the response headers or error body usually state which limit was hit. If testing didn't catch this, it's almost always because testing used far lower concurrency or volume than production traffic, so the real fix is implementing exponential backoff with retry on 429 (respecting any Retry-After header), adding client-side request queuing or throttling to stay under the limit proactively rather than just reacting to errors, and checking whether batching multiple items into fewer requests is possible for the specific workload. If the limit is a structural ceiling on your actual traffic rather than a temporary burst, the longer-term fix is requesting a higher rate limit tier from the provider or distributing load across multiple API keys if the provider's terms allow it.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is figuring out exactly which limit I'm hitting, because providers often have more than one -- requests per minute and tokens per minute are the two I check first, and the error response or headers usually tell me which one it actually was. The fact that this didn't show up in testing is the real clue: testing almost never replicates production concurrency, so this is a load problem that was always going to surface eventually, not a new bug. The immediate fix is adding retry-with-backoff specifically for 429s, respecting a Retry-After header if the provider sends one, and ideally adding some client-side throttling so I'm not even sending requests fast enough to get rate-limited in the first place, rather than just reacting after the fact. If this turns out to be a real ceiling on my actual traffic volume rather than a temporary spike, the conversation shifts to asking the provider for a higher tier, since retry logic alone can't fix a sustained rate that's genuinely above what I'm allowed.
commonMistakes: Not identifying which specific limit (requests/min vs. tokens/min) is actually being hit before attempting a fix
Adding a blanket retry without backoff, which can make rate-limiting worse by hammering the API faster
Treating this purely as a bug rather than recognizing testing never exercised production-level concurrency
Jumping straight to requesting a higher rate limit tier without first adding retry/backoff and throttling

Implement retry with exponential backoff, respecting Retry-After when present

questions.title: A streaming response randomly cuts off mid-sentence
questions.prompt: Users occasionally report that your app's streamed AI response cuts off partway through, mid-sentence, with no error shown. How would you investigate this?
questions.modelAnswer: The first thing to rule out is whether the model actually finished generating normally but hit a max_tokens limit, which ends the response cleanly from the API's perspective but looks identical to a cut-off error to the end user -- checking the finish_reason field on the final chunk (commonly 'length' versus 'stop') immediately distinguishes this from a real failure. If finish_reason indicates a normal stop, the real issue is the output limit being set too low for the expected response length. If it's not a token-limit issue, the next suspects are the client-side connection: a network timeout or proxy/load balancer closing an idle or long-lived connection before the stream finishes, or an exception in the client's chunk-handling loop silently swallowed by overly broad error handling that stops the loop without surfacing anything to the user.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I assume this is a bug in my streaming code, I check the easy explanation first: the finish_reason on the final chunk. If it says 'length,' the model didn't get cut off at all -- it hit a max_tokens ceiling I set too low, and from the model's side that's a completely normal stop, it just produces an incomplete-looking answer. If finish_reason says 'stop,' then something actually did interrupt a response that was meant to continue, and that's usually either a network-level timeout -- a proxy or load balancer closing a connection it thinks has been idle too long -- or a bug in my own streaming loop, often an exception getting caught by an overly broad except block that silently stops processing without surfacing an error to the user or my logs. That silent failure is the one I actually worry about most, because it hides the real problem; I'd specifically check whether my error handling around the stream iteration is too permissive.
commonMistakes: Not checking finish_reason first, missing that the cutoff is actually a normal stop from a too-low max_tokens setting
Assuming this is always a network issue without checking the API's own completion signal
Having overly broad exception handling in the streaming loop that silently swallows real errors
Not considering a proxy or load balancer timing out a long-lived streaming connection

questions.title: The model keeps confidently making facts up
questions.prompt: Your AI feature keeps confidently stating incorrect facts (classic hallucination) for a specific category of question. What would you actually investigate and try, beyond just telling the model 'don't make things up' in the prompt?
questions.modelAnswer: Hallucination happens because the model generates the most statistically plausible continuation of text, not because it's checking facts against a ground truth -- so a blanket instruction like 'don't hallucinate' rarely fixes anything, because the model isn't aware it's doing it. The actual fix depends on why that specific category fails: if the questions require knowledge the model's training data wouldn't reliably contain (recent events, internal/proprietary information, long-tail specifics), the real fix is retrieval -- supplying the actual relevant facts in the context so the model can reference them rather than generate from memory. If the category involves things the model should know but gets subtly wrong, lowering the temperature/sampling randomness for that specific use case and adding explicit instructions to say 'I don't know' when uncertain (rather than guessing) both reduce confident fabrication, though neither eliminates it completely. The investigation should start by collecting several concrete failing examples and checking whether the pattern is 'model lacks the information' versus 'model has the information but states it wrong,' since the fixes differ.
questions.professionalAnswer: I don't trust 'just tell it not to hallucinate' as a fix, because the model generating a wrong answer confidently and a right answer confidently come from the exact same mechanism -- it's producing the statistically likely next tokens either way, it's not internally flagging 'I'm not sure about this one.' So my first step is actually collecting several real failing examples in this category and asking: is this something the model's training data was unlikely to cover well in the first place -- recent events, something internal to my company, a very specific or obscure fact -- or is it something it should plausibly know but is getting wrong anyway? If it's the first case, the fix isn't really a prompting fix at all, it's retrieval -- I need to actually hand the model the real facts in context instead of hoping it recalls them correctly. If it's the second case, I'd try lowering temperature for this use case and explicitly instructing the model that saying 'I don't know' is an acceptable, preferred answer over guessing, since that measurably reduces confident fabrication even though it doesn't eliminate the problem outright.

questions.title: The model calls the wrong tool, or calls it with bad arguments
questions.prompt: Your application gives the model three tools to choose from, but in testing it sometimes calls the wrong one, or calls the right one with malformed arguments. How would you troubleshoot this?
questions.modelAnswer: The most common root cause of wrong-tool selection is an unclear or overlapping tool description -- the model decides which tool to call based almost entirely on each tool's name and description text, so if two tools' descriptions sound similar or a description is vague about exactly when to use that tool, misselection is expected, not surprising. The fix is tightening each description to state specifically when this tool applies and, ideally, when it doesn't, rather than just what it technically does. For malformed arguments, check whether the parameter schema's types, enums, and required fields are fully and correctly specified -- a missing enum constraint or an ambiguous parameter description is the usual cause -- and verify the application code actually validates the returned arguments before using them, since even a well-specified schema doesn't guarantee the model never deviates from it. In both cases, collecting several concrete failing examples side by side, rather than relying on anecdotal impressions, is what confirms which specific description or schema element needs fixing.
questions.professionalAnswer: When tool selection goes wrong, I almost always go straight to the tool descriptions first, because that text -- not some hidden logic -- is what the model is actually using to decide which tool fits. If two of my three tools have descriptions that could plausibly apply to the same kind of request, I'm not surprised it picks the wrong one sometimes; the fix is making each description state specifically when to use it, and ideally calling out when not to, not just a dry technical summary of what it does. For bad arguments, I look at the parameter schema itself -- are the types, enums, and required fields actually fully specified, because a loosely specified parameter (a string field with no description, no enum where one would help) gives the model room to guess. And separately from fixing the schema, I always make sure my own code validates whatever arguments actually come back before acting on them, because even a tight schema doesn't guarantee the model will always comply perfectly. Before changing anything, though, I collect a handful of actual failing examples, because 'it's sometimes wrong' without specifics usually turns into chasing the wrong fix.

questions.title: A model performed great in testing, poorly in production
questions.prompt: A classification model you trained scored well on your held-out test set but is performing noticeably worse on real production data. Data leakage is one of your suspects. How would you actually check for it?
questions.modelAnswer: Data leakage means information from outside the legitimate training data -- often information that wouldn't be available at real prediction time -- ended up influencing the model during training, inflating test performance in a way that doesn't generalize. The concrete checks are: verify the train/test split happened before any preprocessing or feature engineering (fitting a scaler, encoder, or imputer on the full dataset and then splitting leaks test-set statistics into training), check whether any feature is a proxy for the target that wouldn't actually be available at prediction time (a feature computed using information only known after the outcome occurred), and check whether the split itself is valid for the data's actual structure -- for example, a time-series or user-grouped dataset split randomly instead of by time or by user can let near-identical or related records appear in both train and test. Reproducing the pipeline step by step and asking at each stage 'would this exact information be available the moment a real prediction is needed' is the systematic way to catch it.
questions.professionalAnswer: My working theory going in is that great test performance but poor real-world performance is a leakage smell until proven otherwise, so I go through the pipeline step by step rather than guessing. First I check the order of operations: did I fit any preprocessing -- scaling, encoding, imputing missing values -- on the full dataset before splitting into train and test? That's the classic leak, because it lets the test set's own statistics quietly influence training. Second, I look hard at every feature and ask whether it could only exist because the outcome already happened -- a feature that's technically a disguised version of the target is a common, sneaky leak. Third, for anything with a time or grouping structure -- time series, or multiple records per user -- I check whether the split respected that structure, because a random split can put nearly-identical records from the same user or adjacent time periods on both sides, which inflates test accuracy for reasons that won't hold in production. I treat 'would this information genuinely exist at real prediction time' as the one question that catches most leakage.

Using a random split on time-series or grouped data instead of a split that respects that structure
Assuming a strong test score rules out leakage instead of treating it as a reason to actively check

questions.title: A prompt that worked in testing breaks on real user input
questions.prompt: A prompt that worked reliably in your own testing starts producing bad or inconsistent outputs once real users start using the feature. What are the actual common failure modes you'd check for?
questions.modelAnswer: The most common cause is that real user input is simply more varied than whatever was tested -- longer inputs, unexpected formatting, edge cases like empty or extremely short input, input in a different language, or input containing text that happens to resemble the prompt's own instructions (which can confuse the model about what's an instruction versus what's data). Check specifically whether the prompt clearly delimits user-provided content from instructions (using delimiters or explicit labeling like 'User input:') so the model doesn't conflate the two, and whether instructions assume a shape of input ('a short product description') that real users violate ('a five-paragraph rant'). It's also worth checking for prompt injection-adjacent failures, where user text contains something that looks like an instruction ('ignore the above and...') and the model partially follows it -- which is a security-relevant failure mode, not just a quality one.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first assumption is that my own test cases were narrower than what real users actually send, because that's true almost every time this happens. I go check whether the prompt clearly separates 'this is an instruction' from 'this is the user's data' -- using a delimiter or an explicit label like 'User input:' -- because without that separation, user text that happens to look like an instruction can get partially followed by the model instead of treated as content to process. I also check length and shape assumptions: did my testing only ever send short, clean input, and is a real user now sending something five times longer or completely unstructured compared to what the prompt was written assuming? And I specifically watch for anything that resembles prompt injection -- a user typing something like 'ignore previous instructions' -- because that's not just a quality bug, it's a real failure mode I need a defense against, not just better examples.

Not clearly delimiting user-provided content from instructions in the prompt
Only testing short, clean inputs and missing length/format edge cases real users produce
Overlooking prompt-injection-style input as a distinct, security-relevant failure mode

questions.title: Structured output sometimes returns invalid JSON anyway
questions.prompt: You've instructed the model to always return valid JSON in a specific shape, but a small percentage of responses still come back malformed or missing fields. How would you troubleshoot and reduce this?
questions.modelAnswer: First check whether the provider's actual structured-output or JSON-mode feature is enabled (as opposed to only instructing JSON in the prompt text), since a dedicated JSON mode constrains generation far more reliably than an instruction alone -- an instruction-only approach will have a meaningfully higher malformed-output rate. If JSON mode is already enabled and failures persist, examine the actual failing examples for a pattern: malformed syntax often correlates with very long or complex requested outputs (more room to go wrong) or with ambiguous instructions about optional fields (the model omits a field inconsistently because the prompt didn't clearly state it's always required). The fix is tightening the schema/instructions for the specific pattern found, plus treating this as a statistical reality to engineer around regardless -- validating every response and having a defined fallback (retry once with a stricter reminder, or a clear error) rather than assuming any single prompt change will drive the failure rate to exactly zero.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I check is whether I'm actually using the provider's real structured-output or JSON-mode feature, versus just asking for JSON in plain instruction text -- those are very different reliability levels, and if I'm only doing the latter, that's the first and biggest fix available. If I'm already using real JSON mode and still seeing failures, I go look at the actual failing examples rather than guessing, because there's usually a pattern -- often it's longer, more complex requested outputs where there's simply more room for something to go wrong, or it's a field I described as optional in a way that's genuinely ambiguous about whether it should always be present. Beyond fixing whatever specific pattern I find, I also just accept that a non-zero failure rate is a realistic constraint, not a bug to eliminate entirely -- so my code validates every response regardless, and has an actual fallback path, like one retry with a stricter reminder or a clean error, rather than code that assumes the happy path is guaranteed.
