questions.title: Installing one package broke three others
questions.prompt: You run pip install on a new package your project needs, and suddenly several other packages in the environment are broken or behaving unexpectedly. What happened, and how would you actually fix and prevent this?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a dependency conflict: the newly installed package required a different version of a shared dependency than what was already installed and relied on by other packages, and pip silently upgraded or downgraded that shared dependency to satisfy the new package, breaking whatever else depended on the old version's behavior or API. The immediate diagnostic step is checking pip's own output from the install (it often warns about incompatible versions) or running pip check, which reports dependency conflicts in the current environment. The real fix, and the actual prevention, is not installing packages directly into a shared or global environment at all -- using a dedicated virtual environment (venv) per project isolates dependencies so one project's package conflicts can't affect another, and pinning versions in requirements.txt makes the environment reproducible so this kind of surprise is caught before deployment, not discovered live.
questions.professionalAnswer: What almost certainly happened is that the new package needed a different version of something I already had installed, and pip changed that shared dependency to satisfy the new install, which is exactly the kind of thing that quietly breaks other packages that assumed the old version's behavior. My first diagnostic step is just running pip check, which specifically reports version conflicts in the current environment, rather than trying to guess from the symptoms. But honestly, the deeper issue is usually that I wasn't in an isolated environment to begin with -- if I'd had this project in its own venv, a conflict here would only affect this one project's dependencies, not whatever else I have installed globally. Going forward, I treat venv-per-project as non-negotiable, and I pin versions in requirements.txt specifically so a conflict like this shows up as an explicit, visible resolution error when I try to install, instead of pip silently picking a version for me and breaking something I wasn't even looking at.

questions.title: Async code that isn't actually running concurrently
questions.prompt: You wrote async code to call three AI APIs concurrently using asyncio.gather, but when you measure it, the total time is basically the same as calling them one at a time. What's likely wrong, and how would you confirm it?
questions.modelAnswer: The most common cause is that one of the 'async' functions being awaited is actually making a blocking, synchronous call internally -- for example, using a synchronous HTTP client (like plain requests) inside a function marked async def, instead of an actual async-capable client. Marking a function async def doesn't make the code inside it non-blocking; it just makes the function awaitable -- if the body still does synchronous I/O, that call blocks the entire event loop for its duration, which serializes all the 'concurrent' tasks anyway since none of the others can run while the event loop is blocked. To confirm this, check every I/O call inside each task for whether it's genuinely using an async library (an async HTTP client, not requests) and awaiting it properly; a quick way to catch the symptom is adding timestamps before and after each task starts and completes -- if they start and finish sequentially rather than overlapping, that confirms something is blocking the event loop.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is almost always the same root cause: something inside one of those 'async' calls is actually a blocking, synchronous operation -- the classic version is calling the regular requests library inside a function that's technically declared async def. Declaring a function async doesn't magically make its internal work non-blocking; it just means the function can be awaited. If the actual network call inside is synchronous, it blocks the whole event loop while it runs, and since there's only one event loop, nothing else -- including my other two 'concurrent' tasks -- can make progress during that time, so I end up with sequential behavior wearing async syntax. To confirm it, I'd log a timestamp right before and after each task's main call and look at whether the three tasks' time windows overlap at all; if they're back to back instead of overlapping, that's the blocking-call signature. The actual fix is swapping whatever synchronous client is being used inside those tasks for a real async-capable one.

questions.title: You accidentally committed an API key
questions.prompt: You realize you just pushed a commit containing a real API key in a config file to a shared GitHub repository. Walk through exactly what you'd do, in order.
questions.modelAnswer: The single most important and time-sensitive step is revoking/rotating the actual API key at the provider immediately, before doing anything else with git -- the key is compromised the moment it's pushed, regardless of what happens to the repository afterward, since it may already be visible to anyone with access or to any automated secret-scanning bot watching public repos. Only after the key is dead does cleaning up the repository matter: simply deleting the file in a new commit or using git revert is not sufficient, because the key remains fully visible in the git history of the earlier commit; actually removing it from history requires rewriting history (tools like git filter-repo or BFG Repo-Cleaner) and force-pushing the cleaned history, which requires coordinating with any collaborators who may have already pulled the exposed commit. Going forward, the prevention is adding the config file (or a .env pattern) to .gitignore and using a secrets-management approach (environment variables, a secrets manager) instead of committing credentials into any file at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: The very first thing I do, before touching git at all, is go revoke and rotate that key at the provider. That has to happen immediately, because the moment it was pushed it's compromised -- it doesn't matter yet whether I clean up the repo, because the actual exposure already happened and the key needs to stop being valid right now. Only after that's done do I worry about the repository itself, and I'm clear with myself that just deleting the file in a new commit or reverting doesn't actually fix anything -- the key is still sitting in the history of that earlier commit for anyone to find. Actually removing it means rewriting history with something like git filter-repo and force-pushing the result, and since that rewrites shared history, I'd give anyone else working on the repo a heads-up before doing it, because their local clones will now be out of sync with the rewritten history. And longer term, I make sure that config file is in .gitignore and that real secrets live in environment variables or an actual secrets manager, not in a file that can be committed in the first place.

questions.title: Tests pass locally but fail only in CI
questions.prompt: Your test suite passes every time on your own machine, but the same tests fail consistently in GitHub Actions. How would you troubleshoot this?
questions.modelAnswer: The first and most common suspect is an environment difference: check that the CI workflow pins the exact same language/runtime version used locally, since a default or different version can change behavior; check whether all dependencies are actually declared (a package installed locally by hand, outside requirements.txt, works locally but is missing in the clean CI environment, which installs strictly from the declared dependency file). The next suspect is state that exists locally but not in CI's clean environment -- a local environment variable, config file, or cached data the tests implicitly depend on but that was never committed or set in the workflow's env. Reading the actual CI failure logs carefully (not just 'it failed') almost always shows which of these it is -- a missing module error points to dependencies, an authentication or config error points to missing environment variables or secrets, and a different error entirely can point to a version mismatch.
questions.professionalAnswer: My instinct here is that CI is actually telling me the truth and my local machine is the one with hidden, undeclared state -- CI runs from a clean environment every time, so if something only works locally, it's relying on something that exists on my machine but was never actually captured in the repo or the workflow config. First thing I do is actually read the CI failure log carefully rather than just seeing 'failed' and guessing -- a ModuleNotFoundError usually means something I have installed locally never made it into requirements.txt, an auth or config-related error usually means an environment variable or secret I have set locally isn't configured in the GitHub Actions workflow, and a totally different error can point to a Python version mismatch between my machine and whatever the workflow specifies. I treat 'works for me, fails in CI' as the environment being the bug, not the test, and the fix is almost always making the CI environment's actual dependencies and config match what my code genuinely needs, not special-casing CI to work around it.

questions.title: Designing a reusable AI API client class
questions.prompt: You're designing a reusable client class that your whole team will use to call an AI provider's API. What responsibilities should that class actually own, beyond just making the raw HTTP call?
questions.modelAnswer: A well-designed client class should own: authentication (holding the API key and attaching it correctly to every request, so callers never handle it directly), retry logic with backoff for transient failures (429s, 5xxs) so every caller gets consistent, correct retry behavior instead of reimplementing it inconsistently, consistent error handling that translates provider-specific error responses into a clear, predictable exception type for the rest of the codebase, and a clean public interface that returns simple, extracted values (text, parsed structured output) rather than leaking the provider SDK's raw response objects into calling code -- which matters because it means swapping providers later only requires changing the client class internals, not every call site. Things it generally should not own are business logic specific to one feature (prompt construction for a specific use case belongs at the call site, not baked into the shared client) or anything that would make the class harder to reuse across different parts of the application.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think about this as drawing a clear boundary around what's truly shared infrastructure versus what's specific to one feature. The client class should own authentication, so no caller ever touches the API key directly; retry-with-backoff for 429s and 5xxs, so I'm not rewriting that logic slightly differently in five different places; and translating whatever error shape the provider returns into one consistent exception type my codebase understands, rather than every caller needing to know the provider's specific error format. I also make sure its public methods return clean, already-extracted values -- plain text, a parsed dict -- not the raw SDK response object, because that's what actually lets me swap providers later by only touching this one class. What I deliberately keep out of it is anything specific to one feature, like a particular prompt template -- that belongs at the call site, not baked into shared infrastructure that every part of the app depends on.
commonMistakes: Having every caller handle authentication, retries, or error translation independently instead of centralizing it
Returning raw provider SDK response objects instead of clean extracted values, leaking provider-specific shape everywhere
Baking feature-specific business logic (like one use case's prompt template) into the shared client class
Not giving the class a consistent error type, forcing callers to handle the provider's raw error format
keyPoints: The client should centralize authentication so callers never handle API keys directly
Retry/backoff logic belongs in the client, ensuring consistent behavior everywhere it's used
Provider errors should be translated into a consistent, codebase-specific exception type
The client returns clean extracted values, not raw SDK objects, to keep provider swaps localized

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies authentication as a centralized responsibility
Correctly identifies retry/backoff as a centralized responsibility
Correctly identifies consistent error translation as a responsibility
Correctly distinguishes shared infrastructure from feature-specific logic that shouldn't live here

questions.title: Webhooks vs. polling for a long-running AI job
questions.prompt: You're integrating with a provider's API for a job that takes minutes to complete (like a large batch job or a fine-tuning run). The provider supports both polling a status endpoint and webhooks. Which would you architect your system around, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: Webhooks are the better architectural fit for a long-running job: the provider pushes a notification to your endpoint the moment the job's status changes, so you find out as soon as it's actually done, with no wasted requests and minimal added latency between completion and your system noticing. Polling requires your system to repeatedly ask 'is it done yet,' which means choosing a polling interval that trades off between responsiveness (polling too infrequently delays noticing completion) and wasted load (polling too frequently generates many requests that return 'still running'). The real tradeoff against webhooks is infrastructure complexity: webhooks require exposing a publicly reachable endpoint, handling retries if your endpoint is briefly down, and verifying the webhook's authenticity (typically via a signature), which is genuinely more setup than a polling loop. A reasonable middle ground some systems use is polling as a fallback safety net alongside webhooks, in case a webhook delivery is ever missed.
questions.professionalAnswer: For something that takes minutes, I'd reach for webhooks if the infrastructure supports it, because polling for a multi-minute job means I'm either checking way more often than useful and generating a lot of 'still running' responses, or checking infrequently enough that I add real delay between the job actually finishing and my system noticing. Webhooks flip that around -- the provider tells me the instant something changes, so I'm not guessing at a polling interval at all. The real cost of webhooks isn't conceptual, it's infrastructure: I need a publicly reachable endpoint, I need to verify the webhook's signature so I'm not just trusting any POST request that shows up claiming to be from the provider, and I need to handle the case where my endpoint was briefly down when the webhook fired. In practice, I've seen teams keep a slow backup poll running alongside webhooks specifically to cover that last case, so a missed webhook delivery doesn't mean a job result silently never gets picked up.
commonMistakes: Choosing polling for a long-running job without weighing the interval tradeoff between responsiveness and wasted requests
Choosing webhooks without acknowledging the real infrastructure cost (public endpoint, signature verification, retry handling)
Not considering a fallback poll alongside webhooks in case a delivery is missed
Treating this as purely a style preference rather than an architectural tradeoff with real costs on both sides
keyPoints: Webhooks notify immediately on completion, avoiding the polling-interval tradeoff entirely
Polling requires balancing responsiveness against wasted 'still running' requests
Webhooks carry real infrastructure cost: a public endpoint, signature verification, and retry/downtime handling
A fallback poll alongside webhooks is a reasonable hedge against missed webhook delivery

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recommends webhooks for this scenario with sound reasoning
Correctly explains the polling-interval tradeoff
Correctly names the real infrastructure costs of webhooks
Mentions a fallback/hybrid approach as a realistic hedge

questions.title: Designing for a paginated API response
questions.prompt: You need to fetch all records from an API endpoint that returns paginated results (a few hundred pages, each with a cursor or page token). How would you architect the code that walks through all the pages, and what would you watch out for?
questions.modelAnswer: The right structure is a loop that makes a request, processes or yields that page's results, extracts the next-page cursor/token from the response, and uses it as input to the next request, continuing until the response indicates no further pages exist (commonly a null/absent next-token field, rather than assuming a fixed page count). Architecturally, this should be wrapped as a generator function (yielding each page or each item) rather than collecting everything into one giant list in memory first, especially for a few hundred pages, since that keeps memory usage bounded and lets calling code start processing results before the entire fetch completes. Watch for: rate limiting across many sequential requests (this pattern can trigger 429s if not throttled), a request failing partway through (needing either to resume from the last known cursor rather than restarting from page one, or robust retry per page), and the API's pagination contract specifically -- cursor-based pagination behaves differently from offset-based pagination, and assuming the wrong one breaks the loop silently if pages start repeating or skipping records.
questions.professionalAnswer: I build this as a generator, not a function that returns one big list, because a few hundred pages of accumulated results sitting in memory before I even start processing them is wasteful and makes the whole operation feel slower than it needs to be -- yielding each page (or each item) lets the caller start working through results immediately. The loop itself is simple: request a page, process it, pull the next cursor out of the response, and keep going until the API tells me there isn't a next page -- I never assume a fixed total page count going in. What I actually watch out for in practice is rate limiting, since a few hundred sequential requests can trip a provider's limits if I don't add some throttling between them, and failure recovery -- if request 150 of 300 fails, I want to resume from that cursor, not restart the whole walk from page one. I also double check whether the API's pagination is cursor-based or offset-based specifically, because treating one as the other is a subtle bug that can silently skip or duplicate records instead of failing loudly.
commonMistakes: Collecting all pages into memory before processing instead of streaming/yielding results as they arrive
Assuming a fixed total page count instead of relying on the API's own 'no more pages' signal
Not handling a mid-walk failure by resuming from the last cursor, forcing a restart from page one
Confusing cursor-based and offset-based pagination contracts, silently skipping or duplicating records
keyPoints: A generator-based loop processes pages incrementally instead of loading everything into memory first
The loop should rely on the API's own next-page signal, not an assumed fixed page count
Rate limiting across many sequential requests needs explicit throttling
Failure recovery should resume from the last known cursor, and the pagination contract (cursor vs. offset) must be respected

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a generator/streaming approach rather than loading everything into memory
Correctly describes relying on the API's next-page signal
Addresses rate limiting across many sequential requests
Addresses failure recovery/resumption and pagination contract correctness

questions.title: Choosing a model based on cost, latency, and quality
questions.prompt: You're building a feature that classifies thousands of support tickets per day into categories. How would you think through the cost/latency/quality tradeoff when choosing which model to use?
questions.modelAnswer: For a high-volume, structurally simple task like ticket classification, the right default assumption is that a smaller, cheaper, faster model in a provider's lineup is likely sufficient, since classification into a fixed set of categories doesn't typically require the strongest general-reasoning capability a frontier flagship model offers -- and at thousands of calls per day, the per-call cost difference between a flagship and a smaller model compounds into a significant total cost difference. The right approach is to actually measure: build a small evaluation set of representative tickets with known correct categories, run it against both a cheaper/faster model and a stronger one, and compare actual accuracy -- only pay for the stronger, more expensive, typically slower model if the measured quality gap on this specific task is large enough to justify the added cost and latency at this volume. Latency matters here too if classification blocks something user-facing (like auto-routing a ticket in real time) versus running as an offline batch process, which changes how much latency is actually tolerable.
questions.professionalAnswer: My default assumption going in is that I probably don't need the most expensive, most capable model for straightforward classification into a fixed set of categories -- that's not a task that usually needs frontier-level general reasoning, and at thousands of calls a day, even a small per-call cost difference adds up to real money over a month. But I don't just assume that and ship it -- I build a small evaluation set of real tickets with known correct labels, run it through a cheaper/faster model and a stronger one, and compare actual measured accuracy side by side. If the cheaper model's accuracy is close enough for this use case, that's the one I ship, because the cost and latency savings at this volume are real. The other factor I check is whether this classification needs to happen synchronously in a user-facing path or can run as a batch job -- if it's blocking a real-time flow, latency matters a lot more than if it's just running in the background, and that can shift the decision even if the cheaper model's accuracy is slightly lower.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to the most capable/expensive model without evaluating whether the task actually requires it
Not building an actual evaluation set to measure the real quality gap between model options
Ignoring how total cost compounds at high call volume
Not considering whether the use case is latency-sensitive (synchronous) or latency-tolerant (batch)
keyPoints: A simpler, cheaper model is often sufficient for structurally simple tasks like fixed-category classification
Cost differences compound significantly at high call volume
The decision should be based on a measured evaluation, not an assumption about model quality
Whether the use case is synchronous/user-facing or batch changes how much latency actually matters

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons that a cheaper/smaller model is a reasonable starting assumption for this task
Proposes building an actual evaluation set to measure the real tradeoff
Correctly accounts for cost compounding at volume
Considers latency sensitivity based on synchronous vs. batch use

questions.title: Fine-tune or just write a better prompt?
questions.prompt: A stakeholder suggests fine-tuning a model to fix a quality problem in your AI feature. Before agreeing, what would you actually want to check or try first, and when would fine-tuning genuinely be the right call?
questions.modelAnswer: Fine-tuning is a bigger, more expensive, and more operationally demanding commitment than prompting -- it requires curated training data, ongoing maintenance as the base model is updated or deprecated, and re-running the fine-tuning process to incorporate new examples -- so the right default is exhausting simpler fixes first: improving the prompt itself (clearer instructions, few-shot examples), trying a different model in the same task, and adding retrieval/grounding if the problem is a knowledge gap rather than a behavior gap. Fine-tuning genuinely becomes the right call when the need is a specific, consistent behavior or style that's hard to fully specify through examples in a prompt every time (because it would need an impractically long prompt to convey), when the task's output needs to be faster/cheaper than what a flagship model plus a long prompt would cost per call at your actual volume, or when you have a large, well-curated dataset of the exact desired input/output behavior that prompting with a handful of examples can't fully capture.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I'd agree to fine-tuning, I'd want to actually try the cheaper options first, because fine-tuning isn't just a one-time cost -- it's an ongoing commitment to maintaining training data and re-running the process whenever the base model updates or I need new behavior. So first I'd push on the prompt itself: clearer instructions, better few-shot examples, maybe a different model entirely, and if the problem is really a knowledge gap rather than a behavior gap, retrieval instead of fine-tuning altogether. Fine-tuning earns its place when none of that is enough -- specifically when I need a very particular, consistent behavior or style that would take an unreasonably long prompt to fully specify every single call, or when I'm at high enough volume that a shorter fine-tuned model's lower per-call cost and latency actually outweighs the fine-tuning investment, or when I genuinely have a large, high-quality dataset of exactly the input/output behavior I want that a handful of in-prompt examples just can't convey. I wouldn't jump to it as a first move.
commonMistakes: Agreeing to fine-tune before exhausting simpler fixes (better prompting, different model, retrieval)
Treating fine-tuning as a one-time cost rather than an ongoing maintenance commitment
Not distinguishing a knowledge-gap problem (needs retrieval) from a behavior/style problem (candidate for fine-tuning)
Jumping to fine-tuning without a large, well-curated dataset to actually support it
keyPoints: Fine-tuning should come after exhausting simpler fixes: better prompting, model choice, retrieval
Fine-tuning is an ongoing maintenance commitment, not a one-time fix
It's the right call for a specific, hard-to-prompt-for behavior/style, or for cost/latency at scale
A large, well-curated dataset of the desired behavior is a prerequisite for fine-tuning to work well

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly lists simpler alternatives to try before fine-tuning
Correctly frames fine-tuning as an ongoing commitment, not a one-time fix
Correctly identifies legitimate scenarios where fine-tuning is the right call
Distinguishes knowledge-gap vs. behavior-gap problems

questions.title: What to check in a model card before choosing a pretrained model
questions.prompt: You're choosing a pretrained model from a model hub for a specific task in your application's architecture. What would you actually check in its model card before committing to it?
questions.modelAnswer: A model card's most architecturally relevant sections are: the intended use and known limitations (whether the model was actually trained/evaluated for a task close to yours, versus a related but different one), the training data description (what domain and language it covers, which affects whether it will generalize to your actual input distribution), reported evaluation metrics on relevant benchmarks (giving a concrete, comparable sense of expected performance rather than a vague capability claim), the model's size and resource requirements (whether it fits your actual inference infrastructure and latency budget), and licensing terms (whether the license actually permits your intended commercial or production use, which is a real blocker if overlooked). Skipping the limitations and license sections specifically is a common and costly mistake, since a capable-looking model can be legally unusable for your case or can fail in exactly the scenario the card warned about.
questions.professionalAnswer: I go straight to a handful of sections every time rather than skimming the whole card. Intended use and limitations first, because a model that looks great on a general benchmark can have been trained and evaluated on something meaningfully different from my actual task, and the limitations section is usually where that gets spelled out honestly. Then training data, because it tells me whether this model has actually seen data close to what my real inputs look like, or whether I'm extrapolating outside what it was trained for. I check reported metrics against a real benchmark rather than trusting a vague capability claim, and I check size and resource requirements against my actual infrastructure and latency budget, since a model that's too large to run within my latency target is a non-starter regardless of how good it is. And I never skip the license -- I've seen people get well into integration before realizing the license doesn't actually permit the commercial use they needed, which is an expensive mistake to make late.
commonMistakes: Skipping the limitations section and only looking at headline capability claims
Not checking whether the training data domain actually resembles the real input distribution
Ignoring resource requirements relative to actual inference infrastructure and latency needs
Not checking the license, risking a late discovery that commercial/production use isn't permitted
keyPoints: Intended use and limitations reveal whether the model was evaluated for something close to the real task
Training data description indicates whether the model will generalize to the real input distribution
Reported metrics give a concrete performance expectation, not just a general capability claim
Resource requirements and license terms are real, sometimes blocking, architectural constraints

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly checks intended use/limitations against the real task
Correctly checks training data relevance
Correctly checks resource requirements against real infrastructure/latency needs
Correctly checks licensing as a real constraint

questions.title: Managing a context window budget in a multi-turn chat app
questions.prompt: You're architecting a chat application where conversations can run for dozens of turns. How would you manage the context window budget so the app doesn't just break once the conversation gets long?
questions.modelAnswer: The core architectural decision is choosing a strategy for what to send once the full history no longer fits: a sliding window that keeps only the most recent N turns (simple, but can lose earlier important context), summarization that periodically compresses older turns into a shorter summary message that's resent instead of the full original text (preserves gist, loses exact detail), or a hybrid that keeps recent turns verbatim plus a running summary of everything older. Whichever strategy is chosen, the system should track actual token counts (not message counts) against the model's real context window, reserving a fixed budget for the system prompt and the expected response length, and trimming history proactively before a request would exceed the limit rather than reactively handling an error after the fact. The choice of strategy should match the use case: a customer-support bot where exact early details matter benefits more from summarization than a casual assistant where recent context dominates relevance.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I architect for first is tracking actual token counts against the model's real context window, not message counts, because 'keep the last 20 messages' can still blow the budget if those messages happen to be long. Once I have real token accounting, I pick a trimming strategy on purpose rather than by accident: a sliding window of recent turns is simplest and works fine when old context genuinely matters less over time, but for something like a support conversation where an important detail from turn two might still matter at turn forty, I'd rather periodically summarize older turns into a shorter running summary and keep recent turns verbatim, so I'm not just throwing away information the user might reasonably expect the assistant to still know. Either way, I trim proactively before a request would go over budget, reserving headroom for the system prompt and the response itself, rather than waiting for the API to reject an oversized request and handling that as an error case.
commonMistakes: Tracking message count instead of actual token count against the real context window
Only handling context overflow reactively (after an API error) instead of trimming proactively
Always using a simple sliding window regardless of whether early context is actually important for the use case
Not reserving budget headroom for the system prompt and expected response length
keyPoints: Token count, not message count, should be tracked against the real context window
A sliding window and summarization are two distinct strategies with different tradeoffs
Trimming should happen proactively before a request would exceed the limit
The right strategy depends on whether early context is genuinely important for the use case

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly emphasizes real token tracking over message counts
Correctly describes sliding window vs. summarization strategies
Describes proactive trimming with budget headroom
Matches strategy choice to the actual use case

questions.title: Short-term vs. long-term memory for a chat assistant
questions.prompt: Your chat assistant needs to remember things a user said earlier in the same conversation, and ideally also remember facts about the user across separate conversations days apart. How would you architect these two kinds of memory differently?
questions.modelAnswer: Short-term memory -- remembering things within the same conversation -- is solved by resending the conversation history (or a managed, trimmed/summarized version of it) in the context window on every request, since the model itself has no state between calls; this lives entirely within the request/response cycle and disappears once the conversation ends unless explicitly persisted. Long-term memory -- facts that should persist across separate conversations days apart -- requires a separate persistence layer outside the context window entirely: a database or vector store that holds extracted facts about the user, which your application explicitly retrieves and injects into the system prompt or context at the start of a new conversation. These are architecturally distinct because long-term memory isn't just 'a longer context window' -- it requires deciding what's worth remembering (extracting and storing specific facts, not the entire raw conversation), how to retrieve the relevant subset for a new conversation (rather than injecting everything ever learned about the user), and how to handle facts that become outdated or contradicted later.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat these as two genuinely different systems, not one feature. Short-term memory is just conversation history management -- resending the relevant prior turns (trimmed or summarized as needed) in context on every call, because the model has zero memory of its own between requests; that's purely a context-window problem. Long-term memory, remembering things across separate conversations days apart, can't live in the context window at all -- it needs its own persistence layer, typically a database or vector store, where I explicitly extract and store specific facts about the user as they come up, and then retrieve and inject the relevant ones into a new conversation's context when it starts. The hard architectural questions are really in that long-term piece: deciding what's actually worth extracting and storing rather than keeping raw transcripts, retrieving only the relevant subset for the current conversation instead of dumping everything I've ever learned about the user into context, and having a way to update or retire a fact if the user later says something that contradicts it.
commonMistakes: Treating long-term memory as simply 'a bigger context window' instead of a separate persistence layer
Not distinguishing retrieval of relevant facts from injecting everything ever stored about a user
Forgetting that short-term memory requires resending history since the model has no state between calls
Not accounting for facts becoming outdated or contradicted and needing to be updated
keyPoints: Short-term memory is managed conversation history resent within the context window per request
Long-term memory requires a separate persistence layer (database/vector store) outside the context window
Long-term memory requires deciding what to extract/store, not keeping raw transcripts
Retrieval should inject only the relevant subset of stored facts, and should handle outdated/contradicted facts

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly architects short-term memory as managed context/history
Correctly architects long-term memory as a separate persistence layer
Addresses selective extraction and retrieval rather than storing/injecting everything
Addresses updating or retiring outdated facts

questions.title: Structuring a growing AI app instead of one long script
questions.prompt: Your AI feature started as one script that called an API and printed the result. It's since grown to include prompt templates, response parsing, retry logic, and now a second feature using the same API. How would you restructure this with classes, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: The restructuring should separate concerns into distinct classes with clear responsibilities: a client class owning the API call, authentication, and retry logic (shared across both features, since they use the same API); and separate, smaller classes or modules per feature that own their own prompt templates and response-parsing logic specific to that feature's needs, each depending on the shared client rather than duplicating its own copy of the call/retry code. This matters practically once there are two features: without separation, retry logic and API-calling code tend to get copy-pasted and drift out of sync between the two call sites, and a bug fix in one place doesn't automatically apply to the other. With a shared client class injected into each feature, a fix to retry behavior or authentication happens once and both features benefit immediately, and adding a third feature later means writing only its specific prompt/parsing logic, not re-deriving the shared plumbing again.
questions.professionalAnswer: The real signal that it's time to restructure is exactly what happened here -- a second feature showed up needing the same underlying API call. If I don't pull the shared pieces out now, I'm going to copy-paste the retry logic and the API call into the second feature's script, and the moment I need to fix a bug in that logic, I have to remember to fix it in two places, which I will eventually forget to do. So I'd pull the API call, authentication, and retry logic into one shared client class, and then give each feature its own small class or module that owns just what's actually specific to it -- its prompt template, its own response parsing -- and have that feature code depend on the shared client instead of reimplementing any part of it. That way a fix to retry behavior happens in exactly one place and both features get it automatically, and when a third feature inevitably shows up, it only needs to write its own specific logic, not rebuild the plumbing from scratch again.
commonMistakes: Duplicating the API-calling and retry logic into the second feature instead of extracting a shared client
Mixing feature-specific prompt/parsing logic into the same class that owns the shared API plumbing
Not recognizing a second feature needing the same API as the concrete trigger to refactor
Over-engineering with excessive abstraction before there's a second real use case to justify it
keyPoints: A shared client class should own authentication, API calls, and retry logic used by both features
Feature-specific logic (prompt templates, response parsing) belongs in its own smaller class per feature
This separation prevents retry/auth bugs from needing to be fixed in multiple places
A second real use case is a legitimate, concrete trigger to refactor, not premature abstraction

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes extracting a shared client class for common API/retry logic
Correctly separates feature-specific logic into its own classes/modules
Explains the concrete maintenance benefit (fix once, applies everywhere)
Frames the refactor as justified by a real second use case, not premature abstraction

questions.title: Choosing a branching strategy for a small team shipping weekly
questions.prompt: You're setting up Git workflow conventions for a small team of four engineers shipping an AI product feature-by-feature, roughly weekly. Would you reach for Git Flow or trunk-based development, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: For a small team shipping frequently, trunk-based development is generally the better fit: engineers work off short-lived feature branches that merge back into main quickly (ideally within a day or two), main stays continuously deployable, and there's no long-lived develop or release branch structure to keep in sync. Git Flow's additional branch types (develop, release, hotfix, feature, in parallel) add real process overhead -- extra merge points, longer-lived branches that drift further from main the longer they live, increasing conflict risk -- that make more sense for a team managing multiple release versions in production simultaneously (like versioned software with long-term support branches) than for a small team shipping one continuously deployed product weekly. The actual decision criterion isn't team size alone, it's release cadence and whether multiple versions need active parallel maintenance; trunk-based fits a single continuously shipped product, Git Flow fits multi-version maintenance.
questions.professionalAnswer: For this specific situation, I'd go trunk-based. With four engineers shipping weekly, short-lived feature branches that merge back into main quickly keep main always close to what's actually been built and tested, and there's no develop/release branch structure to keep synchronized, which is pure process overhead this team doesn't need. Git Flow's extra branch types earn their complexity when you genuinely have multiple versions of a product in production at once needing separate maintenance -- think versioned software with long-term support branches -- but for a team shipping one continuously deployed product, that structure just adds more places for things to drift and more merge points where conflicts can pile up the longer a branch lives. My actual decision rule isn't about team size by itself, it's about release cadence and whether there are multiple live versions to maintain in parallel -- and this team has neither, so the lighter-weight trunk-based approach is the better fit.
commonMistakes: Choosing Git Flow by default without weighing it against the team's actual release cadence
Not recognizing that Git Flow's extra branch types exist to serve multi-version maintenance needs
Assuming team size alone, rather than release cadence and version-maintenance needs, drives the decision
Not mentioning that longer-lived branches increase merge conflict risk the longer they live
keyPoints: Trunk-based development fits a small team with frequent, continuous releases of one product
Git Flow's extra branch structure is justified by multi-version parallel maintenance needs
The real decision criterion is release cadence and version-maintenance needs, not team size alone
Short-lived branches reduce merge conflict risk compared to longer-lived ones

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recommends trunk-based development for this scenario with sound reasoning
Correctly explains when Git Flow's structure would actually be justified
Identifies the real decision criterion (release cadence/version maintenance), not just team size
Mentions merge conflict risk relative to branch lifespan

questions.title: A stakeholder wants a new field added mid-sprint
questions.prompt: Your team is three days into a two-week sprint when a stakeholder asks you to add a new field to a report you're already building, saying it's 'quick, shouldn't change anything.' Walk me through how you'd actually handle this request.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't just say yes or no -- it describes a specific process for evaluating a mid-sprint request honestly before committing to it. First, actually assess the request rather than taking 'quick' at face value: does the new field require touching the dataset's underlying query, does it interact with existing filters or parameters, does it need its own testing? Second, be transparent with the stakeholder and the team about the real tradeoff: if it genuinely is small, say so and fold it in; if it's not, explain specifically why (not vaguely) and present the actual options -- add it now and risk the sprint's committed work, or add it to the next sprint, or (if it's urgent) swap it in for something already committed and explicitly deprioritized. The point to get across is that this isn't about being rigid or unhelpful -- it's about making the tradeoff visible instead of silently absorbing scope and then explaining later why other committed work slipped.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just say yes because it's described as quick, and I also wouldn't flatly refuse because 'that's not what we committed to' -- I'd actually go look at what the change requires first. If it really is a one-column addition to an existing dataset with no filter interactions, I'd just do it and move on, because treating every tiny request as a formal change-control event is its own kind of overhead. But if it touches the dataset's query, interacts with parameters already in play, or needs real testing, I'd say that specifically and honestly, rather than agreeing and then quietly having something else slip. I'd lay out the actual choice for the stakeholder and my Product Owner: we can add this now and something else committed to this sprint moves to next sprint, or this goes into the next sprint's backlog, or if it's genuinely urgent, I'll tell you specifically what I'd need to drop to make room for it. What I'm protecting isn't my own workload -- it's the team's ability to make an honest commitment and actually hit it, instead of everyone quietly absorbing 'just one more small thing' until the sprint's real scope bears no resemblance to what was planned.
commonMistakes: Automatically agreeing to the request without actually assessing its real scope first
Refusing rigidly without explaining the real tradeoff or offering alternatives
Silently absorbing the extra work and letting already-committed work slip without telling anyone why
Not involving the Product Owner or team in the actual tradeoff decision
keyPoints: Actually assesses the request's real scope instead of taking 'quick' at face value
Is transparent about the tradeoff rather than silently absorbing scope creep
Presents concrete options (do it now and drop something, defer it, or swap priorities)
Frames the goal as protecting the team's ability to make honest commitments, not personal workload

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes actually assessing the request's real scope rather than assuming
Shows transparent communication about the tradeoff involved
Presents concrete, realistic options rather than a flat yes/no
Frames this as protecting the team's commitments, not personal convenience

questions.title: Communicating a blocker in the daily standup
questions.prompt: You're stuck on a task -- a stored procedure change you need is waiting on another team's approval -- and it's been blocked for two days. How would you bring this up in the daily standup, and what would you do about it outside of standup?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats the Daily Scrum correctly -- as a short team sync, not a status report to a manager -- and keeps the standup update itself brief and specific: what's blocked, who or what it's waiting on, and how long it's been stuck, rather than a long explanation of the underlying technical problem. The real work happens outside standup: actually escalating the blocker rather than just mentioning it and waiting -- following up directly with whoever owns the approval, looping in the Scrum Master if the blocker is specifically the kind of cross-team obstacle they're meant to help clear, and being honest with the team about the sprint-goal impact if it stays stuck much longer, rather than quietly hoping it resolves itself. The key distinction a strong answer draws is between mentioning a blocker (passive) and actively working to clear it (what's actually expected).
questions.professionalAnswer: In standup itself, I'd keep it tight: 'I'm blocked on the stored procedure change -- it's been waiting on sign-off from the other team for two days now, and I don't have a resolution plan yet.' That's it -- standup isn't the place to walk through the technical details or vent about how annoying the wait is; it's a quick sync so the team knows where things stand. The actual work happens right after standup, not during it. I'd go directly to whoever on the other team owns that approval and ask specifically what's holding it up and when I can expect it, rather than just waiting passively for two more days. If that doesn't move things, I'd loop in my Scrum Master specifically, because clearing exactly this kind of cross-team blocker is their job, not something I should be expected to just push through alone. And if it looks like this is going to threaten the sprint goal, I'd say that out loud to the team well before the sprint review, not as a surprise at the end -- being blocked isn't a failure on my part, but sitting on it quietly without escalating would be.
commonMistakes: Treating the standup as the place to explain the full technical backstory instead of a brief status
Mentioning the blocker in standup but then passively waiting instead of actively escalating it afterward
Not involving the Scrum Master, whose job specifically includes clearing cross-team blockers
Waiting until the sprint review to surface that the blocker threatened the sprint goal
keyPoints: The Daily Scrum update should be brief and specific, not a technical deep dive
Mentioning a blocker in standup isn't the same as actively working to clear it
Escalating directly to the other team and/or the Scrum Master is the appropriate next step
Sprint-goal risk should be surfaced early, not held until the sprint review

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes an appropriately brief, specific standup update
Describes actively escalating the blocker outside of standup, not just waiting
Correctly involves the Scrum Master's actual role in clearing blockers
Shows early, honest communication about sprint-goal risk

questions.title: Two stakeholders both want their ticket done first
questions.prompt: You have two open tickets: a bug fix a sales manager is pushing for urgently, and a new report feature your own manager assigned last week with a deadline that's actually sooner. Both stakeholders think their request is the priority. How do you handle it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't unilaterally decide between two stakeholders' competing priorities on its own authority -- it recognizes that prioritization decisions belong with whoever actually owns the backlog's priority order (a Product Owner, in Scrum terms, or whoever plays that role on the team), and surfaces the conflict to them explicitly rather than quietly picking one and hoping the other doesn't notice. The practical first step is gathering the actual facts needed to make the decision -- how urgent is the bug really (is it actively breaking something for users right now, or just annoying), and what's the real deadline and consequence of missing it for the report feature -- rather than just taking either stakeholder's framing of urgency at face value. Then bring both pieces of information to whoever should decide, make the conflict and the tradeoff explicit, and get an actual decision rather than silently deprioritizing one person's request without them knowing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to quietly referee this myself between two people who each think their thing is most important -- that's not actually my call to make alone, and if I just pick one, I've effectively made a business priority decision without the authority or the full context to make it well. My first step is getting the real facts: is this bug actually breaking something in production right now, or is it an annoyance that feels urgent but isn't actually blocking anyone? What's the real, hard deadline on the report feature, and what actually happens if it slips a few days? Once I have real answers instead of just each stakeholder's own sense of urgency, I'd go to whoever actually owns prioritization for my work -- my manager, or a Product Owner if that's how the team is structured -- lay out both asks and their actual urgency side by side, and ask for an explicit call. I'd rather spend ten minutes getting a clear decision than spend a day guessing which stakeholder to disappoint and then having to explain that choice after the fact.
commonMistakes: Unilaterally deciding between two stakeholders' competing priorities without the authority or full context to do so
Taking either stakeholder's self-reported urgency at face value instead of verifying the actual impact and deadline
Quietly deprioritizing one request without telling that stakeholder, letting them find out later
Not escalating to whoever actually owns prioritization decisions for the team's work
keyPoints: Prioritization conflicts between stakeholders should be escalated, not unilaterally resolved
Gathers real facts about urgency and deadlines rather than accepting either framing at face value
Brings both pieces of information to whoever owns the priority decision for an explicit call
Avoids silently deprioritizing a stakeholder without their knowledge

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes this isn't a unilateral decision and escalates appropriately
Describes gathering real facts about urgency/impact before escalating
Describes a clear, explicit escalation with both pieces of information presented
Avoids silently disappointing either stakeholder without communication

questions.title: A ticket has no acceptance criteria
questions.prompt: You pick up a ticket from the sprint backlog that says 'Add a filter for region to the sales dashboard' with no further detail -- no acceptance criteria, no mention of default behavior or how it should interact with existing filters. What do you do before writing any code?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer resists the temptation to just start building based on a guess, because a story without acceptance criteria is genuinely too vague to know when it's actually done -- 'I think this is done' and a shared, checkable definition of done are different things, and building against the wrong assumption wastes real time for both the developer and whoever has to send it back. The right move is going back to whoever owns the ticket -- the Product Owner or the stakeholder who requested it -- and asking specific, concrete questions rather than one vague 'what do you mean': what should the filter's default value be, does it need to interact with (cascade from or into) any existing filters already on the dashboard, and is there a specific list of regions or should it reflect whatever's in the data. Writing those answers down as explicit acceptance criteria before starting, not after, turns a vague request into something both the developer and whoever reviews the finished work can actually check against.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start building off a guess, because 'add a filter for region' sounds simple but actually hides several real decisions -- what region data source is sensible as the dropdown's default, whether this filter needs to interact with any filter already on the dashboard, whether 'region' even means the same thing across every table the dashboard touches. Guessing wrong on any of those means I build something, it gets reviewed, and it comes back with changes -- which is slower overall than just asking upfront. So before writing anything, I'd go back to whoever owns the ticket with specific questions, not a vague 'can you clarify this' -- I'd ask directly: should this default to the viewer's own region if we track that, does selecting a region need to affect any other filter already on the page, and is there an existing region list I should match or is this open-ended. Once I have real answers, I'd write them down as the ticket's acceptance criteria myself if nobody else does, specifically so there's a shared, checkable definition everyone agrees to before I start -- that protects me too, since I now have something concrete to point back to if the request changes later.
commonMistakes: Starting to build based on a guess instead of clarifying ambiguous requirements first
Asking a vague 'can you clarify this ticket' instead of specific, concrete questions
Not writing down the clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria before starting
Assuming the ticket's brevity means the request is actually simple, missing the real decisions hidden inside it
keyPoints: A story without acceptance criteria is genuinely too vague to know when it's actually done
Asks specific, concrete clarifying questions rather than a vague request for more detail
Writes down the clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria before starting work
Clarifying upfront is faster overall than building on a guess and having it sent back

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes the ticket is too ambiguous to build from directly
Asks specific, concrete clarifying questions rather than a vague request
Describes writing down clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria
Explains why clarifying upfront saves time overall

questions.title: The Business Says the Dashboard You Built Isn't What They Asked For
questions.prompt: You finish a dashboard, it passes your own testing, and then the business stakeholder reviews it in UAT and says it doesn't actually answer what they needed. How do you respond, and how do you prevent the same gap next time?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats a UAT rejection as a normal, expected signal rather than a personal failure or a sign the stakeholder is being difficult — UAT exists specifically to catch the case where code is technically correct but isn't actually what the business needed, which is a different question than QA's "does it work correctly" entirely. The right immediate response is to ask specific, concrete questions rather than getting defensive: what exactly does the current version show, what were they expecting instead, and can they point to a specific number or view that's wrong relative to their mental model. Often the real gap traces back to acceptance criteria that were vague or incomplete at the start, not a build mistake — which is the actual thing to fix going forward: writing more specific, checkable acceptance criteria during intake (edge cases included, like what a zero-sales region should display) so UAT becomes a confirmation step rather than where requirements gaps first surface.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd do is not get defensive about it, because UAT rejecting something isn't the same as me having done something wrong — it's literally what that stage is for, catching the gap between 'this is technically correct' and 'this is actually what we needed,' which are genuinely different questions. I'd ask specific questions rather than just apologizing and reworking blindly: what exactly were you expecting to see here, can you show me a specific number that looks wrong to you versus what you expected. Usually when I dig into it, the real root cause isn't that I built the wrong thing technically — it's that the original request or acceptance criteria were vague enough that I made a reasonable assumption that just wasn't the assumption they were making. Going forward, the actual fix isn't 'be more careful next time,' it's writing tighter, more specific acceptance criteria up front — including the edge cases, like what happens when a region has zero sales for the month — so that gap gets caught during planning instead of surfacing for the first time in UAT.
commonMistakes: Treating a UAT rejection as a personal failure or getting defensive instead of investigating specifically
Reworking the dashboard based on a vague complaint without asking specific clarifying questions first
Not tracing the root cause back to incomplete acceptance criteria, repeating the same gap on the next project
Assuming the stakeholder is simply wrong instead of taking their feedback as a genuine signal about the request
keyPoints: UAT exists specifically to catch 'technically correct but not what was needed,' a different question than QA
The right response is specific clarifying questions, not defensiveness or blind rework
The root cause is often vague acceptance criteria at intake, not a build mistake
The real fix is tighter acceptance criteria going forward, including edge cases

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Responds professionally and non-defensively to the rejection
Describes asking specific clarifying questions
Correctly identifies the likely root cause (acceptance criteria gap)
Proposes a concrete prevention for next time
